content: Miscarriage is defined as the loss of a pregnancy before 23 weeks of gestation. It occurs in approximately 10% to 15% of pregnancies, with the likelihood varying based on maternal age and parity. Chromosomal abnormalities are implicated in about half to two-thirds of all cases of miscarriage. Various interventions have been proposed to prevent miscarriage, but bed rest is one of the most frequently recommended strategies, particularly in cases of threatened miscarriage or a history of previous miscarriage. However, since the majority of miscarriages are not caused by excessive physical activity, it is unlikely that bed rest would be an effective method to prevent spontaneous pregnancy loss. The objective of this review was to assess whether prescribing bed rest during pregnancy is effective in preventing miscarriage in women who are at high risk of pregnancy loss. To address this, a search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register as of March 2010. The review included all published, unpublished, and ongoing randomized controlled trials that reported clinical outcomes for pregnant women who were prescribed bed rest either at home or in a hospital setting, compared to alternative care or no intervention. Two independent reviewers evaluated the methodological quality of the included studies using the guidelines outlined in the Cochrane Reviewers' Handbook. Studies were included regardless of their methodological rigor. Ultimately, only two studies involving a total of 84 women met the inclusion criteria. The results of the analysis showed no statistically significant difference in the risk of miscarriage between women who were prescribed bed rest and those who received no bed rest (either placebo or other treatments). The calculated risk ratio (RR) was 1.54, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) ranging from 0.92 to 2.58. Additionally, there was no significant difference in miscarriage prevention between women who were prescribed bed rest at home versus those prescribed bed rest in a hospital setting. However, women in the bed rest group had a higher risk of miscarriage compared to those who received human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) therapy without bed rest (RR 2.50, 95% CI 1.22 to 5.11). The small sample size of the included studies is a major limitation, making it difficult to draw definitive conclusions from the analysis. Based on the available evidence, there is insufficient high-quality data to support the routine prescription of bed rest as a strategy to prevent miscarriage in women with confirmed fetal viability and vaginal bleeding during the first half of pregnancy.
